vignette:
Elena's Testimony

Elena sits with her hands folded in her lap, her gray-streaked hair pulled back neatly, the posture of someone accustomed to public composure. At fifty-eight, she carries herself with the authority of someone who has spent the last decade navigating city politics, yet something in her eyes suggests she's still elsewhere-still in the place she left behind fifteen years ago.

She was forty-three when she took a leave from her position as a community liaison officer to work with an international relief organization in a region fractured by conflict. She wanted to do something that mattered, she explains, something beyond the incremental negotiations of municipal governance. For eight months, she coordinated medical supply distribution and helped establish temporary clinics in areas where fighting had displaced thousands. The work was difficult but purposeful. She felt needed in a way her city council position never quite achieved.

The attack came without warning. A mortar round struck the compound where she and two colleagues were cataloging medications. She remembers the sound first-not like anything she'd heard before, a percussion that seemed to come from inside her own body. Then the smell of dust and burning. One colleague died instantly. The other was airlifted out with severe injuries. Elena was physically spared, though a piece of shrapnel grazed her shoulder, leaving a thin scar she still sometimes touches without meaning to.

She returned home after a brief hospitalization. People called her brave. She was invited to speak at community events about her service. She resumed her council position. On the surface, she functioned. But the functioning required an architecture of avoidance she built without fully acknowledging it.

She stopped attending evening city council sessions, citing scheduling conflicts. Loud noises-fireworks, backfiring cars, even slamming doors-sent her into a state of hypervigilance that could last hours. She found herself unable to sit in the middle of rooms; she positioned herself always near exits. Meetings with constituents became exhausting; she couldn't focus on their concerns because part of her attention remained elsewhere, scanning for threats. She started taking longer and longer drives at night, alone, the only time her mind felt quiet.

The insomnia crept in gradually. She'd lie awake at three in the morning replaying the moment before the blast, a loop of if only-if only they'd finished the inventory an hour earlier, if only she'd suggested they work outside, if only she'd insisted her colleague take a different assignment. She knows logically that survival wasn't something she controlled, yet her mind refuses to accept this.

Over the past five years, the symptoms have settled into a pattern she's learned to manage but not overcome. She attends council meetings but rarely speaks. She's declined two opportunities to run for mayor. She maintains a careful social distance from colleagues, finding group gatherings increasingly intolerable. The hypervigilance has become her baseline; she no longer notices when she's doing it. She's stopped going to restaurants with open layouts. She no longer drives to the waterfront where she used to find peace.

What troubles her most is the disconnection. She looks at photographs from before the deployment and feels she's looking at someone else's life. Her sister invited her to a wedding last month; Elena attended but felt absent, watching herself from outside her body. She's never discussed the full weight of this with anyone-not her family, not her colleagues in city government who still regard her as the woman who served overseas.

She describes all of this in measured tones, as though reporting on a constituent's complaint. Only her hands betray her-they're trembling slightly as she speaks.
